entries.meaning: The forest region held countless hermitages, like a populous land of cities, towns, villages, and hamlets. Its abundant strange birds and animals formed an indescribable citizenry. Deer, tigers, and boars were warriors, while buffaloes and bulls displayed the equipment of an army. Abandoning enmity, all grazed together here and there like a fourfold host. Cascades poured and rutting elephants trumpeted as though many kinds of drums and standards sounded. Cakravākas, cakoras, cātakas, parrots, cuckoos, and swans called sweetly with glad hearts; bees sang and peacocks danced, as though blessing surrounded a well-governed realm. Every vine, tree, and blade of grass bore fruit and flowers, and the whole company was a source of joy and blessing. Beholding the beauty of Rāma’s mountain, Bharata’s heart overflowed with love, like an ascetic happy when the completed vow yields its fruit.

Guha climbed to a height, ran forward, raised his arm, and told Bharata: ‘Lord, look at those immense trees—pākara, rose-apple, mango, and tamāla. Amid those excellent trees a banyan shines, lovely and vast enough to enchant the mind. Its foliage is deep blue and dense, its fruit red, and its unbroken shade pleasant in every season. It seems a gathered mass of darkness suffused with dawn-red beauty, as though the Creator had concentrated loveliness into it. These trees stand near the river, Lord, where Raghubara’s leaf hut is roofed. Around it are various fine holy basil plants, some set by Sītā and some by Lakṣmaṇa. Beneath the banyan Sītā built a platform with her own lovely lotus hands. There Sītā and wise Rāma sit daily with sages and hear narratives and histories from Āgamas, Vedas, and Purāṇas.’

Hearing his friend, Bharata looked toward the trees and tears surged into his eyes. The two brothers bowed as they advanced, while even Sarasvatī would hesitate to describe their love. They rejoiced at the marks of Rāma’s feet as a pauper might upon finding the philosopher’s stone. They placed the dust upon their heads, hearts, and eyes and experienced happiness equal to meeting Raghubara. Bharata’s indescribable state drew even animals, birds, and insentient life into love’s absorption. Overcome by affection, he lost the path, while gods indicated the right way by raining flowers. Perfected beings and practitioners saw his attachment and began praising his innate love. Who on earth could have brought forth Bharata’s feeling, making the unmoving move and the moving stand still? Love’s nectar was Mount Mandara, separation the churning rope, and Bharata the deep ocean; churned for gods and saints, that ocean revealed the compassionate Raghubīra.

Lakṣmaṇa did not notice the charming pair approaching with their friend, concealed by dense forest. Bharata saw the Lord’s sacred hermitage, lovely abode of every blessing; entering it extinguished his burning sorrow, as when a yogin attains the highest aim. Lakṣmaṇa stood before the Lord, answering questions in loving speech. His head bore matted hair and his waist an ascetic cloth; his quiver was fastened, arrow and bow in hand and upon the shoulder. Upon the altar Raghurāja shone with Sītā amid an assembly of sages and saints. His dark body, matted locks, and bark garment appeared like Kāma himself dressed as an ascetic. Turning bow and arrow in lotus hands, he looked on with a smile that removed the heart’s burning. In the lovely circle of sages, Sītā and Raghucandra shone as embodied devotion and existence-consciousness-bliss within an assembly of knowledge.

Bharata, Śatrughna, and Guha became so absorbed that joy and grief and every count of pleasure and pain were forgotten. Crying, ‘Protect me, Lord! Protect me, master!’ they fell flat upon the ground like staffs. Lakṣmaṇa recognized the loving voice and understood in his heart that Bharata was prostrating. On one side brotherly love overflowed; on the other, he was bound by service to his master. He could neither go meet Bharata nor remain where he stood; even a fine poet cannot express Lakṣmaṇa’s mind. He stayed only by placing the weight upon service, like a player’s bird held aloft upon a taut cord. Bowing his head to earth, he lovingly announced: ‘Raghunātha, Bharata is paying homage.’ On hearing, Rāma rose in love’s agitation, scattering garment, quiver, bow, and arrows. The abode of grace forcibly raised Bharata and clasped him to his heart; seeing their meeting, everyone forgot self-consciousness.

How can the brothers’ loving meeting be described? It is beyond the deeds, mind, and speech of the whole lineage of poets. Both were full of supreme love and forgot mind, intellect, awareness, and ego. Tell me: who can manifest such pure love, and whose shadow could a poet’s understanding follow? A poet has only the limited strength of meanings and syllables, like an actor dancing in imitation of rhythm and cadence. Bharata and Raghubara’s unfathomable love is a place even the minds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva cannot reach; how could one of poor understanding tell it? Could a barren reed sound a melodic mode upon a wire instrument? Seeing their meeting, the gods trembled in fear; Bṛhaspati awakened and reassured them, and they showered flowers in praise. Guha lovingly met Śatrughna and then Rāma; Lakṣmaṇa bowed while Bharata embraced him with profound affection.

Lakṣmaṇa eagerly embraced his younger brother Śatrughna, and Rāma again drew Guha to his heart. Bharata and Śatrughna then bowed to the sages and joyfully received the blessings they desired. Surging with love, Bharata placed the pollen of Sītā’s lotus feet upon his head. As he repeatedly bowed, she raised him, touched his head with lotus hands, and seated him. Sītā blessed him inwardly; immersed in affection, he had no awareness of his body. Seeing Sītā favorable in every way, he became free of worry and inward fear. No one said or asked anything: hearts were filled with love and emptied of their ordinary movement. At that moment Guha steadied himself, joined his hands, prostrated, and submitted: ‘Lord, the mothers, citizens, servants, army commanders, ministers, and all others have come with the chief sage, distraught by separation.’

Hearing of the guru’s arrival, Rāma—the ocean of gracious conduct—left Sītā near Śatrughna and hastened out, bearing steadfastness, duty’s weight, and compassion for the lowly. Seeing the guru, he and Lakṣmaṇa lovingly began full prostrations; the eminent sage ran, raised them into his heart, and embraced both as love surged. Thrilling with devotion, Guha announced his name and bowed flat from a distance; Vasiṣṭha forcibly embraced Rāma’s friend, as though gathering affection that rolled upon the earth. The sky praised devotion to Raghupati, source of every blessing, and gods rained flowers. Who could be more utterly low in social standing than Guha, and who in the world greater than Vasiṣṭha? The joyful sage met him even more warmly than Lakṣmaṇa: such is the manifest glory and power of worshiping Sītā’s Lord.

Rāma knew every distressed person, for the compassionate, discerning Lord understood the wish in each heart and responded to each according to that feeling. Meeting everyone with Śatrughna in a moment, he removed their terrible burning sorrow. This is no great feat for Rāma, just as one sun appears in millions of vessels. Meeting Guha with overflowing love, all the citizens praised his fortune. Rāma then saw the grieving mothers, like rows of tender vines struck by frost. He first approached Kaikeyī; his simple nature and devotional understanding remained unchanged. Falling at her feet, he consoled her again, assigning the fault to time, action, and destiny. Raghubara met all the mothers and satisfied them with reassurance: ‘Mother, the world is subject to the Lord; blame should be laid upon no one.’

The two brothers bowed at the feet of the guru’s wife and the wives of brahmins who had come with her. They honored every woman like Gaṅgā and Gaurī, and the women gladly gave gentle blessings. Clinging to her feet, they entered Sumitrā’s lap like paupers meeting immense wealth. Then both brothers fell at their mother’s feet with every limb overwhelmed by love. With profound affection Kausalyā clasped them to her heart and bathed them with tears of love. How could a poet describe the mingled joy and sorrow of that moment, any more than a mute person can describe a taste? After Raghurāya and Śatrughna had met their mother, Rāma asked the guru where the travelers should camp. By the great sage’s order the citizens inspected water and dry land and settled in suitable places. Taking brahmins, ministers, mothers, guru, and chosen people, Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa, and Raghunātha went toward the sacred hermitage.
